questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{2x} & ⇒ & v=\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}-\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}x{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}(x{e}^{2x}){|}_{0}^{1/2}-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x{e}^{2x}){|}_{0}^{1/2}-\frac{{e}^{2x}}{4}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1/2)}-0\cdot {e}^{2\cdot 0}]-\frac{1}{4}[{e}^{2(1/2)}-{e}^{2\cdot 0}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{e}{2}-0]-\frac{1}{4}[e-1] \\  & =\frac{e}{4}-\frac{e-1}{4} \\  & =\frac{e-e+1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⇒ & v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =2[\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & +2[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =2[-\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}]+2[0-0] \\  & =2(-2\pi )+0 \\  & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x+1\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (6x+1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =(6x+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 6\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =(6x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-6\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(6x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+6\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot (-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))-\int (-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{4}{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0))+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)) \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }(-1-0)+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}(0-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$
